title: A Theoretical Bridge Between Long-Tailed Recognition and Continual Learning
claim: A learning problem can be recast as a sequential one, so standard methods inherit a provable bound on the original objective.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, large bridge arrows between colored boxes
description: Three rounded panels, red, blue and green, run left to right. They are linked by block arrows labeled "Bridge to CL" and "Theoretical Guarantee". Panel 1, "Training under LTR", shows a long-tailed bar histogram split into Head and Tail. Beside it is a contour plot where the full-weights optimum sits close to the head-weights optimum, with the note Distance ∝ 1/√IF. Panel 2, "CLTR", shows partitions (Head, Tail 1, Tail 2) mapped by arrows to sequential tasks that prevent forgetting. Below that is a Venn diagram with ψ_H, ψ_HT and ψ_T. A green CL path is contrasted with a red dashed naive fine-tuning path. Panel 3 shows two stacked loss surfaces, with the CL objective above and the balanced objective below, linked by green arrows and the inequality L_CL ≥ L_bal. Theorem labels appear throughout. The eye goes first to the bold panel titles.
caption: Overview of our framework: (left) theoretical analysis of convergence under the LTR setup, showing how imbalance drives convergence toward head-class solutions; (middle) our proposed CLTR reformulating LTR as a CL problem; and (right) the conditional optimization guarantee establishing that the CL objective upper-bounds the balanced LTR loss up to an additive constant.
abstract: We theoretically and empirically establish a previously unexplored connection between Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) and Continual Learning (CL). Specifically, we show that training on a long-tailed dataset with imbalance factor $\mathrm{IF}$ drives model parameters into an $O(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{IF}})$ neighborhood of the dominant-class solution, under both uniform and exponentially decaying cardinality distributions. Building on this result, we establish an objective-level reformulation of LTR as a sequential learning problem and prove that the CL objective upper-bounds the balanced LTR loss up to a constant determined by the residual Head loss. Motivated by this connection, we introduce Continual Learning for Long-Tailed Recognition (CLTR), a principled framework that leverages standard off-the-shelf CL methods to sequentially learn Head and Tail classes while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments on CIFAR100-LT, CIFAR10-LT, ImageNet-LT, and Caltech256 validate our theoretical predictions and demonstrate strong performance across diverse LTR benchmarks. In the foundation-model regime, CLTR with DualPrompt on a CLIP backbone outperforms standard adaptation baselines and is competitive with specialized methods using external semantic supervision. Our work bridges LTR and CL both theoretically and empirically, providing a principled approach for addressing long-tailed learning using standard CL strategies.
